I am 61 years old and have been farming these 10 mu of land in Quzhou for 40 years. My father taught me, and now my wife and I manage it alone — our children have gone to the city. I know every patch of this soil. The wheat-maize rotation has never failed me, and I see no reason to change what works.

It is early autumn now, so I will sow winter wheat across the full 10.1 mu right after the National Day holiday. I will use my old rotary tiller to prepare the seedbed properly — the soil needs to be broken up fine for wheat to take root before winter. I will buy improved wheat seed from the county supply shop, the same kind my neighbors use. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. Water is precious even with my well, so I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the crop overwinter, once at jointing in spring when the wheat is thirsty, and once during grain filling. I will spray herbicide after sowing, and maybe one or two more times for insects and disease if the weather turns damp. I expect about 1,000 jin per mu if the spring frost does not bite too hard.

As soon as the wheat comes off the combine in early June, I will plant summer maize the same day — there is no time to waste in the double-crop system. I will use hybrid maize seed, Nongda or Denghai, and sow directly without ploughing to catch the moisture left from the wheat field. Maize needs less fuss than wheat. I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress at the big trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice if the summer drought comes, and spray three times for weeds and corn borer. I expect about 1,100 jin per mu if the summer storms do not flatten it.

This is what I have always done. The land rewards steady hands, not fancy experiments.
